newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Randstad sees profits growth over 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Randstad sees profits growth over 10 pct.

text.p: Randstad Holding NV, the world's fourth largest temporary employment agency, said on Tuesday it expected net profits to grow more than 10 percent in 1997 but declined to be more precise.
"We are in the middle of a good year," chairman Frits Goldschmeding told a news conference on the 1996 annual report.
He said it would be too conservative to expect a profit rise of only 10 percent. The Dutch company announced in February that 1996 profits rose 27 percent to 207 million guilders.

Randstad shares rose 3.70 guilders to 150.20 at 1205 GMT, after hitting a day's high of 152.50, on today's news that it planned a 2.5-for-one share split in the autumn of this year because the value of the shares had risen sharply.
"The stock split is expected to result in higher trading activity for the shares," Randstad said.
Randstad said it was outperforming its markets.
"There is not a single activity or market (country) where we did not gain market share," Goldschmeding said.
Randstad said the market for staffing services in France slipped by five percent last year, while Randstad managed to increase sales by 16 percent in France.
Goldschmeding did not rule out any acquisitions, adding Randstad was on the lookout for medium-sized temp agencies.
He said Randstad was looking at and assessing medium sized companies within Europe.
He said it had looked at French temporary work firm BIS, of which Vendex currently has 93.4 percent.
"We had been discussing BIS for five to six months, but we decided not to buy the firm as we did not have the management capacity to lead this firm," he said.
Most growth is expected to come from organic growth with sales expected to increase fourfold over the next 10 years, Goldschmeding told reporters.
Randstad's turnover was nearly six billion guilders in 1996.
Golschmeding said the sales growth forecast for the next ten years did not take future acquisitions into account.
Asked by reporters if profit growth would keep pace with sales growth, Goldschmeding said it would.
Goldschmeding is to retire in May 1998, when he will be 65.
He said he would retire next year if there was no urgent need to stay on.
